items.front: In Banner, what is the PIDM and why is it the join key for person-level data?
items.back: The PIDM is Banner's internal numeric person identifier. It is assigned once and shared across modules, so person-level tables (SPRIDEN, SPBPERS, SFRSTCR, SGBSTDN and others) all carry a PIDM column and join on it. The visible student ID (SPRIDEN_ID) is a separate attribute.
items.trap: Do not join on the visible ID. It can change, appears in more than one SPRIDEN row where a person has history, and other systems often store it with different formatting. Treat the PIDM as an internal key and use a pseudonymised surrogate in shared outputs.

items.front: SPRIDEN holds name and ID history. How do you get the current row for a person?
items.back: Filter to SPRIDEN_CHANGE_IND IS NULL. Historical rows carry a change indicator (commonly I for an ID change and N for a name change). Also filter SPRIDEN_ENTITY_IND = 'P' if you want persons only, since non-person entities live in the same table.
items.trap: Joining SPRIDEN without the change indicator filter multiplies rows for anyone with a name or ID change, which inflates headcounts silently.

items.front: How are Banner tables named, and what are STV tables?
items.back: Names follow a pattern of system letter, module letter and a type letter. Examples: SPBPERS and SGBSTDN are base tables (B), SPRIDEN, SPRADDR and SFRSTCR are repeating tables (R), and STV tables are validation tables, the code lists behind coded columns such as term, status and level (STVTERM, for example).
items.trap: Coded columns hold codes, not descriptions. Join to the relevant STV table (or a dbt seed or dimension built from it) to get readable values, and carry the code as well as the description.

items.front: How do you get the student record that applies to a given term from an effective-dated table such as SGBSTDN?
items.back:
SGBSTDN has a row per person per effective term (SGBSTDN_TERM_CODE_EFF). The row that applies to a term is the one with the greatest effective term that does not exceed it. In Snowflake: filter term_code_eff <= the term, then QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY pidm ORDER BY term_code_eff DESC) = 1.
Newer Banner curriculum data is held in SORLCUR and SORLFOS with sequence numbers and current or active flags. Know which your instance treats as authoritative.
items.trap: Joining term = effective term drops students with no row for that term. Taking the maximum effective term overall picks future-dated rows. Using both SGBSTDN and SORLCUR for the same attributes can double count.

items.front: Why not run analytics straight off the production Banner database?
items.back: It competes with transactional load, the schema is highly normalised, coded values need validation-table joins, many tables are updated in place so history is lost, and access is hard to govern. Replicate into a warehouse (raw layer untouched), build history with snapshots, model with dbt, and serve BI from the modelled layer. Banner's own reporting layers such as the ODS exist, but the same governance and history questions apply.
items.trap: A good answer also covers refresh cadence, how deletes in the source are detected, and how reconciliation to the source system is demonstrated.

items.front: Your enrolment number differs from the figure in last year's published return. What is the most likely cause?
items.back: Official returns use data frozen as at a census or reference date. Live Banner data keeps changing through late registrations, corrections, withdrawals and status changes. Reproducible reporting needs the as-at date stated and snapshots kept, so a historical number can be regenerated.
items.trap: Re-running last year's report on live data and expecting the same answer. Capture snapshots at the census date and report from them for official figures.

items.front: Headcount, enrolments and FTE: what is the difference?
items.back: Headcount counts distinct students. Enrolments (registrations) count student-programme or student-module records, so one student can be counted several times. FTE weights each student by study load. Headcount is not additive across programmes, since a student on two programmes appears in both rows but only once in the total.
items.trap: Summing headcount from rows. Totals need DISTINCTCOUNT at the student grain, and the grain of the fact table must be stated before choosing the measure.

items.front: How do you define and calculate a continuation or retention rate?
items.back: Fix four things first: the cohort (for example entrants to a given year, level, mode and domicile), the follow-up point (still enrolled or qualified at the same census the next year), the exclusions, and the denominator. Retention is retained cohort members divided by the cohort. Regulatory indicators such as the OfS continuation, completion and progression measures have precise definitions, so check the current published methodology rather than relying on memory.
items.trap: Quietly changing the cohort definition between years, or counting new students in the follow-up term as retained.

items.front: How do UK GDPR and disclosure control apply to student analytics?
items.back: Student data includes special category data such as ethnicity, disability and health, so the lawful basis, minimisation, access control and retention need to be defensible and documented (a DPIA for new uses). Small counts can identify individuals, so apply an agreed disclosure-control rule (suppress, round, or aggregate) in the semantic layer, and watch for secondary disclosure through totals and subtotals.
items.trap: Hiding a visual or using conditional formatting does not protect data that is still in the model. RLS filters rows, not small counts.

items.front: How do you reconcile student identities across two systems with no guaranteed shared key?
items.back: Normalise first (trim, case, remove formatting, pad IDs). Match deterministically in tiers: exact shared ID, then ID plus date of birth, then name plus date of birth plus another attribute. Record which rule matched and a confidence level. Route unmatched and ambiguous records to an exceptions table for review. Never auto-merge on name alone, and track match rate over time.
items.trap: Fuzzy matching on names alone creates false positives that are hard to detect and unsafe for student data. Keep a mapping table so decisions are auditable and reversible.

items.front: What are Power Query privacy levels, and what causes the Formula.Firewall error?
items.back: Each source is marked Public, Organizational or Private, which controls whether data from one source may be sent to another when queries are combined. Formula.Firewall appears when a single step both references another query and accesses a data source directly, which could leak data between sources. Fix it by restructuring: one query per source, and a separate query that combines them.
items.trap: "Ignore privacy levels" silences the error but removes the protection. Avoid it for student data.

items.front: What are the trade-offs of a composite model that mixes Import and DirectQuery tables from different sources?
items.back: You get fresh data from a large source alongside fast imported dimensions. Relationships between tables in different source groups are limited relationships: uniqueness is not guaranteed, blank-row handling differs, and RELATED cannot be used across them. Dual storage mode on shared dimensions helps. Cross-source joins can be expensive.
items.trap: Often the better answer is to land all sources in one warehouse and model there. Composite models are a compromise when that is not possible.

items.front: How is on-premises Oracle (Banner) data refreshed in the Power BI service?
items.back: Typically through an on-premises data gateway with the Oracle client software installed on the gateway machine, with the data source and credentials configured in the service, and a refresh schedule. If Banner is replicated into a cloud warehouse such as Snowflake, no gateway is needed for that source.
items.trap: Gateway as a single point of failure and a bottleneck. Mention gateway clustering, monitoring and the case for moving transformation upstream.

items.front: How would you design RBAC for student data in Snowflake?
items.back: Roles by function rather than by person, arranged in a hierarchy (access roles that hold object privileges, granted to functional roles, granted to users). Least privilege, future grants on schemas, separate raw, staging and mart layers, masking policies on sensitive columns, row access policies for faculty or department scoping, secure views for sharing, and a service role for BI with only the access it needs.
items.trap: Granting privileges directly to users, using ACCOUNTADMIN for routine work, or giving the Power BI service account a broad role.

items.front: How do you secure student data in a Power BI semantic model?
items.back: Dynamic RLS using a security table and USERPRINCIPALNAME() to scope by faculty or department. Object-level security to hide sensitive columns or tables from some roles. Sensitivity labels, workspace and app permissions, and sharing viewers rather than editors. Disclosure control for small counts built into measures. Test with real viewer accounts.
items.trap: Relying on hidden pages or report-level filters. Anything in the model can be queried by someone with build access.

items.front: How do you structure and test a dbt project built on Banner data?
items.back: Staging models rename, type and filter each source table (for example current SPRIDEN rows only). Intermediate models hold joins and effective-dating logic. Marts expose facts and dimensions at a declared grain. Tests: unique and not_null on keys, relationships between facts and dimensions, accepted_values on codes, source freshness, and custom tests such as one current identity row per PIDM. Use snapshots for tables updated in place.
items.trap: Business logic buried in staging, no declared grain, and tests only on primary keys.

options.why: Correct. History rows carry a change indicator and the current row does not.

options.why: Activity dates can change on historical rows, so this is unreliable.
This separates persons from non-person entities. It does not distinguish current from historical rows.
A sequence value reflects insertion order, not which row is current.

items.prompt: You are joining SPRIDEN, SFRSTCR and SGBSTDN. Which column should you join on?

options.why: Correct. It is the stable internal person key present in each table.
It can change over time and repeats across SPRIDEN history rows.
Not unique and not present in every table.
Term identifies a period, not a person.

items.prompt: You need each student's SGBSTDN row as it applied in term 202410. Which approach is right?

options.why: Drops students who had no row created in that exact term, even though an earlier row still applies.

options.text: Filter term_code_eff <= '202410', then QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY pidm ORDER BY term_code_eff DESC) = 1
options.why: Correct. It picks the latest row that is effective on or before the term for each student.

options.text: Take MAX(term_code_eff) per student with no term filter
options.why: Returns the latest row overall, which may be future-dated relative to the term.

options.text: Take the row with the latest activity date
options.why: Activity date records when a row was touched, not which term it applies to.

items.prompt: A refresh fails with "Formula.Firewall: Query references other queries or steps, so it may not directly access a data source". What is the underlying cause?

options.text: Wrong credentials for the data source
options.why: Credential failures produce different errors.

options.text: A step both references another query and accesses a data source, which the firewall blocks to prevent data leaking between sources
options.why: Correct. Fix by separating source queries from the query that combines them, or by aligning privacy levels deliberately.
This gives a connectivity error, not a firewall error.

options.text: The result has too many rows
options.why: Row count does not trigger this error.

items.prompt: The fact table has one row per student per programme registration. Which measure gives a correct student headcount at every level including the total?

options.why: Counts registrations, so a student on two programmes is counted twice in the total.
Correct. It counts each student once in whatever filter context applies.

options.text: SUM(Registration[HeadcountFlag]) where the flag is 1 on each row
options.why: Same problem as COUNTROWS. A flag at registration grain double counts.
Counts non-blank programme codes, which is registrations again.

items.prompt: A dashboard shows disability counts by course, and some cells are 1 or 2. What is the most robust control?

options.text: Hide small values with conditional formatting
options.why: The values are still in the model and visible in tooltips, exports and queries.

options.text: Apply the agreed suppression or rounding rule inside the measure, and review totals for secondary disclosure
options.why: Correct. The control is in the semantic layer so report authors cannot bypass it.
RLS restricts which rows a user sees, not whether small counts are disclosed.

options.text: Add a note asking users not to share the report
options.why: A policy reminder is not a technical control.

items.prompt: Your January enrolment count differs from the figure in the official return for the same date. Most likely cause?

options.why: Syntax problems give errors, not plausible but different numbers.

options.text: Your report reads live data, while the return used a frozen snapshot taken at the census date
options.why: Correct. Late changes and corrections to live records move the number. Report official figures from snapshots.
Caching affects freshness of a refresh, not a structural difference of this kind.

options.text: Banner stores times in a different timezone
options.why: Timezones rarely explain a count difference like this.

items.prompt: Analysts need the student table, but only a small group may see date of birth and ethnicity. Best approach in Snowflake?

options.text: Keep separate copies of the table for each audience
options.why: Duplicates data, drifts out of sync, and multiplies the governance burden.

options.text: Apply a masking policy on the sensitive columns that checks the querying role
options.why: Correct. One table, one definition, access controlled by role at query time.

options.text: Hide the columns in Power BI
options.why: Hiding in the report layer does not protect the warehouse and is bypassable.

options.text: Give all analysts a high-privilege role
options.why: Violates least privilege.

items.prompt: A source table is updated in place, so old values are lost, and you need history of changes. Which dbt feature fits?

options.text: An incremental model that appends new rows
options.why: Appends new keys but does not capture changes to existing rows reliably.
Correct. A snapshot records changed rows with validity dates, using a timestamp or check strategy.
A view reflects the current state only.
Seeds are static CSV files in the repository.

items.prompt: You must link student records from Banner to another system. Which matching rule do you apply first?

options.why: Highest false-positive risk. Use only as a flagged last resort.

options.text: Exact match on a shared unique identifier after normalisation
options.why: Correct. Deterministic, explainable and auditable. Lower tiers handle what it misses.
Many students share a birth date.
Households and shared accommodation produce collisions.

items.prompt: In a composite model, an Import dimension is related to a DirectQuery fact table from a different source. What is true of that relationship?

options.text: It is a limited relationship, and RELATED cannot be used across it
options.why: Correct. Cross source group relationships are limited, with weaker guarantees about uniqueness and blank rows.

options.text: It behaves exactly like a normal one-to-many relationship
options.why: Limited relationships differ in important ways.
It can, which is the point of composite models.

options.text: It forces the Import table to DirectQuery
options.why: Storage modes are set per table.

items.prompt: How should you derive academic year, term type and term dates from a Banner term code?

options.text: String maths on the term code in every report
options.why: Term code conventions are institution-specific, so repeated string maths gives inconsistent and often wrong results.

options.text: A governed term dimension that maps each term code to academic year, term type and start and end dates
options.why: Correct. Built once from STVTERM plus your institution's rules, tested, and reused everywhere.

options.text: Use the calendar year of the activity date
options.why: Terms and academic years do not align with calendar years.

options.text: Ask users to select the academic year manually
options.why: Does not solve the derivation.

items.prompt: What does a table visual with Programme on rows show for both measures, including the Total row?
items.code:
Headcount = DISTINCTCOUNT(Registration[StudentID])
Registrations = COUNTROWS(Registration)
items.explanation: The programme rows add to 3 students but the Total row shows 2, because S1 is counted once. Registrations is a row count, so it does add to 3. Headcount is non-additive across programmes.

items.prompt: Month-end headcount snapshots are stored on the last calendar day of each month and the Date table is complete. What do the two measures return?
items.code:
Summed = SUM(Snapshot[Headcount])
Closing = CALCULATE(SUM(Snapshot[Headcount]), LASTDATE('Date'[Date]))
items.explanation: Headcount at a point in time is semi-additive: it sums across students but not across time. At quarter level Summed gives 315, which is meaningless. LASTDATE picks the last date in context (31 Mar), so Closing returns that day's snapshot, 105. If the last day can lack data, use LASTNONBLANK instead.

items.prompt: What do the three measures return?
items.code:
Cohort =
CALCULATE ( DISTINCTCOUNT ( Enrolment[StudentID] ), Enrolment[Term] = "202410" )

Retained =
VAR _Base =
    CALCULATETABLE ( VALUES ( Enrolment[StudentID] ), Enrolment[Term] = "202410" )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        DISTINCTCOUNT ( Enrolment[StudentID] ),
        Enrolment[Term] = "202510",
        TREATAS ( _Base, Enrolment[StudentID] )
    )

Retention % = DIVIDE ( [Retained], [Cohort] )
items.explanation: The 202410 cohort is S1, S2 and S3. In 202510, S1 and S3 are still enrolled, so Retained is 2 and retention is 2/3. S4 is a new student in 202510 and is excluded because TREATAS restricts the follow-up count to cohort members.

items.symptom: After joining names onto the enrolment table, the student count is 3% higher than before the join.
items.code:
select e.pidm, e.term_code, i.spriden_first_name, i.spriden_last_name
from enrolment e
join spriden i on i.spriden_pidm = e.pidm
items.diagnosis: SPRIDEN keeps name and ID history, so a person with changes has several rows. The join returns one row per history row.
items.fix: Add and i.spriden_change_ind is null (and entity indicator 'P' if needed), or build a staging model with one current row per PIDM and add a dbt unique test on pidm.

items.symptom: Merging Banner students with a CRM export on StudentID returns no matches, though the IDs look identical in both tables.
items.code: Merged = Table.NestedJoin(Banner, {"StudentID"}, Crm, {"StudentID"}, "Crm", JoinKind.LeftOuter)
items.diagnosis: Data types or formatting differ. One source holds the ID as text with leading zeros (for example 00123456), the other as a number (123456), or one has trailing spaces. M comparisons are exact and type-sensitive.
items.fix: Standardise the key in both queries before merging, for example Text.PadStart(Text.Trim(Text.From([StudentID])), 8, "0"), and set the column type to text in both. Then verify the match rate.

items.symptom: Spring and summer terms are reported in the wrong academic year in the retention report.
items.code: select left(term_code, 4) as academic_year from sfrstcr
items.diagnosis: This assumes the first four characters of the term code give the academic year. If term codes embed the calendar year, spring and summer terms belong to the academic year that began the previous autumn.
items.fix: Build a term dimension that maps each term code to academic year, term type and dates, test it with accepted_values and relationships tests, and join to it instead of deriving values from strings.

items.symptom: Combining monthly faculty workbooks from a folder gives a column that is null for one month, plus an extra column with data for that month only.
items.code: Combined = Table.Combine(Parsed[Data])
items.diagnosis: Table.Combine matches columns by name. One workbook has a slightly different header (for example "Student ID" instead of "StudentID"), so its values land in a separate column.
items.fix: Standardise headers per file before combining, using Table.RenameColumns with MissingField.Ignore driven by a mapping table, and add a schema check that fails loudly when an unknown header appears.

items.symptom: Headcount by programme is correct, but the Total row is larger than the true number of students.
items.code:
Headcount =
SUMX (
    VALUES ( Programme[Code] ),
    CALCULATE ( DISTINCTCOUNT ( Registration[StudentID] ) )
)
items.diagnosis: The measure adds up per-programme distinct counts. Students on more than one programme are counted once per programme in the total.
items.fix: Use DISTINCTCOUNT(Registration[StudentID]) directly, so the total is a distinct count over all students in context.

keyPoints.Agree the definition first: cohort, follow-up point, exclusions, as-at date

items.prompt: Banner and another system disagree about a student's status. How do you handle it?
keyPoints: Establish the system of record for each attribute and document it
Confirm the records genuinely match before comparing

keyPoints.Understand timing: refresh lag, as-at dates, and late updates

keyPoints: Least privilege and roles by function, not by person
Special category fields masked by default and unlocked by role
Faculty or department scoping through row access or RLS

Audit and logging, retention, and a DPIA for new uses

items.name: Current person row from SPRIDEN
items.scenario: Staging model with one current identity row per person.
items.code:
select
    spriden_pidm       as pidm,
    spriden_id         as student_id,
    spriden_first_name as first_name,
    spriden_last_name  as last_name
from {{ source('banner', 'spriden') }}
where spriden_change_ind is null
  and spriden_entity_ind = 'P'
items.notes: Add a dbt unique and not_null test on pidm. If the test fails, you have duplicate current rows in the source, which is itself a finding to report.

items.name: Student record as at a term
items.scenario: The effective-dated student row that applied in a given term.
items.code:
select *
from {{ ref('stg_sgbstdn') }}
where term_code_eff <= '202410'
qualify row_number() over (
    partition by pidm
    order by term_code_eff desc
) = 1
items.notes: String comparison works because term codes sort lexicographically in YYYYMM style. Check this holds for your codes. Parameterise the term in the model or a macro.

items.name: Unmatched records in either source
items.scenario: Reconciliation report listing students that exist in only one of two systems.
items.code:
select
    coalesce(b.student_id_norm, o.student_id_norm) as student_id_norm,
    case
        when o.student_id_norm is null then 'Banner only'
        when b.student_id_norm is null then 'Other system only'
    end as status
from banner_students b
full outer join other_students o
    on b.student_id_norm = o.student_id_norm
where b.student_id_norm is null
   or o.student_id_norm is null
items.notes: Pair this with a count summary (rows and distinct keys per source, matched, unmatched) so you can show the reconciliation moving over time.

items.name: Student headcount
items.scenario: Count each student once in any context.
items.code: Headcount = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Registration[StudentID] )
items.notes: If a Student dimension has one row per student and the relationship is single direction, COUNTROWS(Student) is an alternative that respects filters from the fact via the relationship only when a filter is applied to the fact side. Know which applies in your model.

items.name: Cohort retention
items.scenario: Share of a base-term cohort still enrolled in a follow-up term.
items.code:
Cohort =
CALCULATE ( DISTINCTCOUNT ( Enrolment[StudentID] ), Enrolment[Term] = "202410" )

Retained =
VAR _Base =
    CALCULATETABLE ( VALUES ( Enrolment[StudentID] ), Enrolment[Term] = "202410" )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        DISTINCTCOUNT ( Enrolment[StudentID] ),
        Enrolment[Term] = "202510",
        TREATAS ( _Base, Enrolment[StudentID] )
    )

Retention % = DIVIDE ( [Retained], [Cohort] )
items.notes: Terms are hard-coded for clarity. A real version takes the base and follow-up terms from disconnected parameter tables. It also needs the exclusions and cohort filters agreed in the definition.

items.name: Closing headcount for a period
items.scenario: Point-in-time headcount that does not sum across time.
items.code:
Snapshot Rows = COUNTROWS ( Snapshot )

Closing Headcount =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( Snapshot[Headcount] ),
    LASTNONBLANK ( 'Date'[Date], [Snapshot Rows] )
)
items.notes: LASTNONBLANK handles periods whose last day has no snapshot. LASTDATE is simpler when snapshots always fall on the last day.

items.name: Small-number suppression and rounding
items.scenario: Apply a disclosure-control rule inside the measure.
items.code:
Headcount Safe =
VAR _n = [Headcount]
RETURN
    IF ( _n < 5, BLANK (), MROUND ( _n, 5 ) )
items.notes: The threshold and rounding must follow your institution's agreed rule. Suppressing cells does not stop disclosure through totals, so check subtotals and consider complementary suppression.

items.name: Virtual relationship to a second source
items.scenario: Count CRM contacts for the students currently in filter context without a physical relationship.
items.code:
CRM Contacts =
CALCULATE (
    COUNTROWS ( Crm ),
    TREATAS ( VALUES ( Student[StudentID] ), Crm[StudentID] )
)
items.notes: Useful when two sources cannot be related directly, such as across source groups in a composite model. Both columns must share the same data type and format, so standardise keys first.

items.name: Standardise a join key across sources
items.scenario: Make IDs from two systems comparable before a merge.
items.notes: Do this in the staging step of each source query, then merge. Check the match rate after the merge rather than assuming it worked.

items.name: Combine workbooks from a folder
items.scenario: Append monthly Excel returns from several departments.
items.code:
let
    Source = Folder.Files("C:\Data\Returns"),
    Xlsx = Table.SelectRows(Source, each [Extension] = ".xlsx" and not Text.StartsWith([Name], "~$")),
    Parsed = Table.AddColumn(
        Xlsx,
        "Data",
        each Table.PromoteHeaders(Excel.Workbook([Content]){0}[Data], [PromoteAllScalars = true])
    ),
    Combined = Table.Combine(Parsed[Data])
in
    Combined
items.notes: Table.Combine matches by column name, so standardise headers per file first. Excel lock files (names starting ~$) must be excluded. Path and sheet index are placeholders.

items.front: Why is AVERAGE(ModuleResult[Mark]) often the wrong average mark for a student or programme?
items.back: It weights every result equally, so a 10-credit module counts the same as a 40-credit one. A credit-weighted mean is SUM(mark x credits) / SUM(credits), where the credits in the denominator are only those on rows that actually have a mark.
items.trap: Including credits for unmarked rows in the denominator drags the average down. Also confirm local rules: whether resit marks are capped, and whether the final mark uses best or latest attempt.

items.front: Students take many modules and modules have many students. How do you model it for Power BI?
items.back: Use ModuleRegistration (or ModuleResult) as the fact at student-module-term grain: Student 1-to-many Registration, Module 1-to-many Registration, both single direction. Filters from either dimension then reach the fact, and measures count through it. A direct many-to-many relationship or a bidirectional filter between Student and Module is the thing to avoid.
items.trap: Bidirectional filters create ambiguous paths and slow queries. If one dimension must filter the other, prefer TREATAS or CROSSFILTER inside a specific measure.

items.front: How do you count students who meet a condition calculated per student (for example 120 credits passed)?
items.back: Iterate the distinct students in context, evaluate a measure for each (context transition does the per-student filtering), keep those that pass the test, then count: COUNTROWS(FILTER(VALUES(Student[StudentKey]), [Credits Passed] >= 120)).
items.trap: Blank compares as zero in DAX, so a student with no rows can pass a test like [Rate] < 0.7. Add NOT ISBLANK where that matters. On large student tables, a precomputed flag in the warehouse is cheaper.

items.front: RANKX over ALL(School[SchoolName]) versus ALLSELECTED(School[SchoolName]): what changes? What about TOPN?
items.back:
The table argument defines who is being ranked. ALL ranks against every school regardless of slicers. ALLSELECTED ranks only within the schools the user has selected. RANKX defaults to descending order and to Skip for ties.
TOPN(5, ...) returns more than 5 rows when values tie at the cut-off, unless you add a tie-breaker expression.
items.trap: A rank measure shows odd values on the total row, so check what you want there, often BLANK via HASONEVALUE.

items.front: How do you handle an academic year that does not match the calendar year?
items.back:
Put academic attributes in the Date and Term tables: AcademicYearStart, a label such as 2025/26, term type, and term start and end dates, sorted with sort-by-column. Calendar year-to-date logic then becomes explicit filters on those attributes.
DATESYTD can take a year-end date string (for example for a 31 July year end), but how that string is read is locale-sensitive, so filtering on a modelled academic year column is the safer route.
items.trap: Using YEAR([Date]) for reporting by academic year splits every year in two.

items.front: What are SELECTEDVALUE and HASONEVALUE used for, and what is the subtle behaviour?
items.back: SELECTEDVALUE(column, alternate) returns the value when exactly one value is visible and the alternate result (blank by default) otherwise. HASONEVALUE tests for exactly one value. Typical uses: dynamic titles, parameters read from a slicer, and measures that only make sense for one programme or term.
items.trap: They respond to filters arriving through relationships as well as direct selections, so a filter on a related table that leaves one row can make the test succeed.

items.front: Why does the BLANK versus zero distinction matter for rates such as attendance?
items.back: Blank means no data (no sessions timetabled), zero means data exists and the answer is zero. DIVIDE returns blank when the denominator is zero or blank, which is usually the honest result. Visuals drop blank rows by default, so the choice changes which students appear, and comparisons treat blank as zero.
items.trap: DIVIDE(a, b, 0) hides the difference and makes students with no sessions look like non-attenders.

items.front: Field parameters or calculation groups: when do you use which?
items.back: Field parameters let a report user switch which measures or columns a visual shows (Headcount, FTE or Registrations; School, Level or Mode on an axis). Calculation groups modify any measure through calculation items using SELECTEDMEASURE, for example Current, Prior Academic Year, and Year-on-Year %, so you write the time logic once.
items.trap: Calculation groups require implicit measures to be disabled, and format strings and precedence need care. Calculation group authoring is easiest in Tabular Editor.

items.front: How do you analyse a distribution of marks in DAX?
items.back: MEDIAN and PERCENTILE.INC for robust summaries, STDEV.S or STDEV.P for spread (sample versus population), and a disconnected bands table (Lower, Upper, label) with a measure that counts marks within the selected band for a histogram.
items.trap: A mean alone hides the shape. Small cohorts make percentiles unstable, so show the n alongside.

items.front: Enrolment rows have school codes that are not in the School dimension. What happens and what do you do?
items.back: Power BI groups those rows under a (Blank) member, which hides the integrity problem in plain sight. Fix upstream: add an Unknown member to each dimension, map unmatched keys to it, and add tests (relationships tests in dbt, and an orphan count surfaced in the report or monitoring).
items.trap: Blank members make totals look right while category breakdowns quietly lose rows.

items.front: What does a well-kept semantic model look like?
items.back: A dedicated measures table or tidy home tables, display folders, consistent naming, descriptions, format strings, hidden keys and technical columns, sort-by-column for month and term labels, a marked date table, auto date/time disabled, and no implicit measures where calculation groups are used.
items.trap: In interviews, mention that someone else must be able to maintain it. Documentation and naming are part of quality.

items.front: Admissions want application numbers updated every few minutes during Clearing. How do you choose the storage mode?
items.back: Import is fastest but only as fresh as the last refresh, and scheduled refresh counts are limited by licence or capacity. DirectQuery gives fresh data but depends on source performance, adds source load, and limits some DAX and modelling features. Hybrid tables (incremental refresh with a real-time partition, on supported capacities) and aggregations are the middle ground. Often the best answer is a narrow, pre-aggregated source view with DirectQuery for the live slice and Import for dimensions (Dual or composite).
items.trap: Also ask what freshness is truly needed and whether the source can handle the query load. Check current licence limits.

items.front: A student-level report with tens of thousands of rows is slow. How do you triage it?
items.back: Measure first. Performance Analyzer isolates the slow visual and splits DAX query time from rendering. Copy the query into DAX Studio and read server timings to separate storage engine from formula engine time. Then reduce visible rows and fields, remove high-cardinality columns, avoid heavy measures inside iterators over Student, check for bidirectional relationships, and push per-student flags and aggregates upstream.
items.trap: Rewriting DAX on a hunch without evidence. Always compare before and after timings.

items.front: Attendance is recorded per session and runs to tens of millions of rows. What do you do?
items.back: Decide what questions need which grain. Aggregate to student-module-week or student-term in the warehouse for the model, and keep session-level detail out of Import (or behind drill-through or aggregations with DirectQuery) unless needed. Smaller grain means a smaller, faster model.
items.trap: Keeping every row because it might be useful later. Cardinality drives model size.

items.front: Why use a shared, certified semantic model instead of many report files with their own data?
items.back: One governed definition of headcount, retention and attainment, built and tested once, used by many thin reports through live connection. Certification signals which one to trust, lineage shows what feeds what, and change control through Git and deployment pipelines applies in one place.
items.trap: Separate PBIX copies drift, and two reports giving different student numbers is the classic university data credibility problem.

items.front: A scheduled refresh has started failing. How do you diagnose it?
items.back: Read the error in refresh history and decide which layer failed. Gateway: offline or outdated. Credentials: expired or changed. Source: timeout, permissions, schema change such as a renamed column. M: type conversion errors or firewall errors. Model: memory or size limits, duplicate keys on the one side of a relationship. Fix the cause, rerun, and add failure notifications.
items.trap: Retrying repeatedly without reading the message.

items.front: How do you promote a semantic model from development to production safely?
items.back: Separate Dev, Test and Prod workspaces connected by a deployment pipeline, with deployment rules that swap the data source and parameters per stage. Keep the model and report in source control through Git integration (the PBIP project format stores them as text), use pull requests for review, and have users run UAT in Test.
items.trap: Deploying without rules leaves Prod pointing at Dev data. Feature names and formats in this area change, so check current documentation.

items.front: Which column do you use for RangeStart and RangeEnd on a Banner-derived table, and what about changed rows?
items.back: Partition on a date that does not change for a given row, such as registration date or term start. A column like ACTIVITY_DATE changes whenever a row is edited, so the same row can end up in two partitions and duplicate. Use the detect-data-changes option with a last-modified column (such as activity date) so only partitions whose data changed are refreshed.
items.trap: The filter on the partition date must fold, or each partition scans the whole table.

items.front: You run a hand-written SQL query as the source of a query. What happens to folding, and is there a fix?
items.back: A native query normally stops folding, so later steps run locally. Value.NativeQuery(Source, "select ...", null, [EnableFolding = true]) can let later steps fold on connectors that support it.
items.trap: A better pattern is a view in the warehouse, so the logic is versioned and testable. Check connector support for EnableFolding.

items.front: When is fuzzy matching in Power Query acceptable?
items.back: For low-risk reference lists, for example mapping free-text department names in departmental spreadsheets to a canonical School list, with a sensible similarity threshold and a transformation table for known variants. Review the matches, and prefer an explicit mapping table once variants are known.
items.trap: Not for matching people. A false match between two students is a data protection incident, not a nuisance.

items.front: How can Snowflake Time Travel help with reconciliation?
items.back: You can query a table as it was at an earlier point inside the retention window (AT or BEFORE with a timestamp or statement), which lets you reproduce a figure published last week, compare before and after a load, or recover from a bad update. Retention defaults to one day and can be longer on higher editions.
items.trap: It is not a substitute for deliberate snapshots. Once the retention window passes the data is gone.

items.front: Banner updates rows in place. How do you keep history for reporting as at a date?
items.back: Two approaches. A periodic snapshot (copy the relevant tables at each census or month end) answers "what did we count on that date" exactly. A type 2 history (dbt snapshots, valid_from and valid_to) answers "which department was this student in at the time of the event" and lets you join facts to the dimension as at the event date.
items.trap: Do not rely on activity dates alone, since they show when a row was touched, not what it said before.

items.prompt: You need a student's credit-weighted average mark. Which measure is closest to correct?

options.why: Weights every result equally regardless of credits.
Correct in principle. Refine it so the denominator only includes credits on rows that have a mark.
Divides marks by credits, which has no meaning.
Averages credits, not marks.

items.prompt: Which measure gives the first-attempt pass rate (pass mark 40)?

options.why: Correct. Numerator and denominator are both restricted to first attempts.
The denominator includes resits, so the rate is understated.
Mixes first attempts and resits in both parts.
Returns a Boolean about the average mark, not a rate.

items.prompt: The Application table has ApplicationDate (active relationship to Date), OfferDate and AcceptDate (inactive). How do you count offers by offer month?

options.why: Correct. The inactive relationship is activated inside CALCULATE, and COUNT skips applications with no offer.
Uses the active relationship, so it counts by application month.
Still reports by application month because the active relationship decides the date.

options.text: Create a bidirectional relationship on OfferDate
options.why: Direction is not the issue, and only one relationship between two tables can be active.

items.prompt: Each head of school should see only their school, and some staff cover several schools. Which RLS design works best?

options.text: One role per school, with each user added to the right role in the service
options.why: Works, but it is a lot of administration and drifts as staff change.

options.text: One role on the School table with a filter that checks a security table (email to school code) using USERPRINCIPALNAME()
options.why: Correct. Dynamic RLS driven by data that the school or governance team can maintain.

options.text: A separate report for every school
options.why: Multiplies maintenance and definitions.

options.text: Hide the other schools on a slicer
options.why: A slicer is not security.

items.prompt: You need the average of each student's own average mark. Which measure does that?

options.why: The average over all marks, which weights students with more modules more heavily.
No context transition, so each student returns the same overall average.
Correct. CALCULATE turns each student into a filter, so the inner average is per student.
Equivalent to AVERAGE over all marks.

items.prompt: A visual shows student headcount by school, and the user has selected two schools in a slicer. Which denominator gives each school's share of the selected schools?

options.why: Includes every school, ignoring the slicer.
Correct. It removes the visual's own row filter but keeps the slicer selection.
Keeps the row filter, so every row returns its own count.
Gives share of itself, always 100 percent.

items.prompt: You want students in the Banner extract that have no matching row in the Enrolment query. Which join kind in Table.NestedJoin?

options.why: Returns only students with enrolments.
Correct. Returns left rows with no match on the right.
Returns all left rows, so you would still need a filter on the null matches.
Returns unmatched rows from both sides.

items.prompt: A departmental return has columns StudentID, ModuleCode, Coursework, Exam, Practical. You want one row per component. The department sometimes adds a new component column. What is the most robust step?

options.text: Select StudentID and ModuleCode, then Unpivot Other Columns
options.why: Correct. New component columns are picked up automatically.

options.text: Select the three component columns and Unpivot Columns
options.why: Hard-codes the column names, so a new component is silently missed.
Swaps rows and columns, not what is needed.
Pivot goes the other way, from rows to columns.

items.prompt:
You want students with no enrolment. This query returns no rows, though you know such students exist. Why?
select student_key from student where student_key not in (select student_key from enrolment)

options.text: enrolment.student_key contains NULLs, so NOT IN evaluates to unknown for every row
options.why: Correct. Use NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN with IS NULL instead.

options.text: NOT IN is not supported in Snowflake
options.why: It is supported.
Data type is not the issue here.

options.text: A DISTINCT is required inside the subquery
options.why: Duplicates do not change the result.

items.prompt: How do you list students with more than three failed attempts (mark below 40)?

options.text: WHERE mark < 40 GROUP BY student_key HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
options.why: Correct. WHERE filters rows before grouping and HAVING filters the groups.

options.text: WHERE mark < 40 AND COUNT(*) > 3 GROUP BY student_key
options.why: Aggregates cannot be used in WHERE.
mark is not grouped or aggregated at that point.
Does not count failures.

items.prompt: A student dimension keeps history with valid_from and valid_to (valid_to is null for the current row). How do you attach the department that applied at the time of each result?

options.text: on r.student_key = d.student_key and r.result_date >= d.valid_from and r.result_date < coalesce(d.valid_to, '9999-12-31')
options.why: Correct. A half-open interval avoids matching two rows at a boundary, and the coalesce handles the current row.
Matches every historical version, so rows multiply.

options.text: on r.student_key = d.student_key and d.valid_to is null
options.why: Gives today's department, not the one at the time.
Matches only results dated exactly when a version started.

items.prompt: You need each student's latest attempt per module. Which expression is correct in Snowflake?

options.text: qualify row_number() over (partition by student_key, module_key order by attempt_no desc) = 1
options.why: Correct. One row per student and module, the highest attempt number.

options.text: qualify row_number() over (partition by student_key order by attempt_no desc) = 1
options.why: Returns one row per student, not per student and module.
A single value for the whole table.

options.text: qualify row_number() over (partition by module_key order by mark desc) = 1
options.why: Returns the top mark per module across all students.

items.prompt: A matrix of 40,000 students with several measures is slow. What is the best first step?

options.why: Spends money before knowing the cause.

options.text: Use Performance Analyzer to isolate the slow visual, then examine its query in DAX Studio (storage versus formula engine)
options.why: Correct. Measure before changing anything.
Removes a control and may not be the cause.
Usually makes things slower, not faster.

items.prompt: Which column is the best partition column for incremental refresh on an enrolment table?

options.text: ACTIVITY_DATE, because it shows the latest change
options.why: It changes when a row is edited, so a row can appear in more than one partition and duplicate.

options.text: A date fixed for the row, such as the registration or term start date, with change detection on the activity date
options.why: Correct. Rows stay in one partition, and changed partitions are still refreshed.
Not a date, so it cannot be used with RangeStart and RangeEnd.
Not a column of the data.

items.prompt: A bar chart by school shows a (Blank) category with 800 students. What is the best fix?

options.text: Filter the blank out of the visual
options.why: Hides the problem and the totals no longer reconcile.

options.text: Map unmatched school codes to an Unknown member in the dimension upstream and test for orphans
options.why: Correct. Fixes the integrity issue at source and makes it visible and monitored.
Loses real records.

options.text: Ignore it, it is only 800 rows
options.why: Unmanaged data quality issues accumulate.

items.prompt: Users want any measure in the model switchable between this academic year, last academic year, and year-on-year change. Best approach?

options.text: A calculation group with calculation items that use SELECTEDMEASURE()
options.why: Correct. The time logic is written once and applied to every measure.
Switches which fields are shown, not how a measure is calculated.
Works but multiplies maintenance.

options.text: Use a slicer on the Date table
options.why: Filters the period, but cannot present prior-year comparison for the same selection.

items.prompt: What does a table visual with Module on rows show, including the Total row?
items.code:
Students Failing =
CALCULATE ( DISTINCTCOUNT ( ModuleResult[StudentKey] ), ModuleResult[Mark] < 40 )
items.explanation: M1 failures are S1 and S2, M2 failure is S1. The module rows add to 3, but the total is a distinct count of students with any failing mark in context: S1 and S2, so 2.

items.prompt: What do the two measures return with no filters?
items.code:
Mean Of All Marks = AVERAGE ( ModuleResult[Mark] )

Mean Of Student Means =
AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( ModuleResult[StudentKey] ), CALCULATE ( AVERAGE ( ModuleResult[Mark] ) ) )
items.explanation: All marks: (80 + 80 + 40) / 3 = 66.7. Student means are 80 and 40, so their average is 60. The first weights S1 twice because S1 has two results.

items.prompt: Three schools have 40, 30 and 30 students. The slicer selects Science and Arts only (Science 40, Arts 30). What do the measures show per row?
items.code:
% Of All = DIVIDE ( [Headcount], CALCULATE ( [Headcount], ALL ( School ) ) )
% Of Selected = DIVIDE ( [Headcount], CALCULATE ( [Headcount], ALLSELECTED ( School ) ) )
items.explanation: ALL(School) includes Law, so the denominator is 100 and the shares are 40% and 30%. ALLSELECTED keeps the slicer, so the denominator is 70 and the shares are 40/70 and 30/70.

items.prompt: ApplicationDate is the active relationship to Date and OfferDate is inactive. What does a table with Month on rows show for both measures, including the Total row?
items.code:
Applications = COUNTROWS ( Application )

Offers =
CALCULATE ( COUNT ( Application[OfferDate] ), USERELATIONSHIP ( Application[OfferDate], 'Date'[Date] ) )
items.explanation: Applications counts by application month: Jan has A1, A2, A4 and Feb has A3. Offers counts by offer month: A1 in Jan, and A3 and A4 in Feb. A2 has no offer and COUNT ignores blanks, so the Total is 3 rather than 4.

items.prompt: What does this query return?
items.code:
select s.student_key, e.academic_year
from student s
left join enrolment e on e.student_key = s.student_key
where e.academic_year = '2024/25'
items.explanation: The LEFT JOIN produces S2 with 2023/24 and S3 with null, but the WHERE clause then removes both, so it behaves like an inner join. To keep all students, move the condition into the ON clause: left join enrolment e on e.student_key = s.student_key and e.academic_year = '2024/25'.

items.prompt: With the T2 term in context, what does each measure return?
items.code:
New Students =
VAR _Now = VALUES ( Enrolment[StudentKey] )
VAR _Start = MIN ( Term[TermStartDate] )
VAR _Before =
    CALCULATETABLE ( VALUES ( Enrolment[StudentKey] ), FILTER ( ALL ( Term ), Term[TermStartDate] < _Start ) )
RETURN COUNTROWS ( EXCEPT ( _Now, _Before ) )

Continuing Students =
VAR _Now = VALUES ( Enrolment[StudentKey] )
VAR _Start = MIN ( Term[TermStartDate] )
VAR _Before =
    CALCULATETABLE ( VALUES ( Enrolment[StudentKey] ), FILTER ( ALL ( Term ), Term[TermStartDate] < _Start ) )
RETURN COUNTROWS ( INTERSECT ( _Now, _Before ) )
items.explanation: T2 students are S2, S3, S4. Earlier terms contain S1 and S2. EXCEPT leaves S3 and S4 (new), INTERSECT leaves S2 (continuing). S1 left before T2 and is in neither.

items.symptom: A calculated column on the Student table shows the same average mark for every student.
items.code:
-- calculated column on Student
Student Avg Mark = AVERAGE ( ModuleResult[Mark] )
items.diagnosis: A calculated column evaluates in row context, which does not filter ModuleResult. Without context transition, AVERAGE sees the whole table every time.
items.fix: Wrap it in CALCULATE: Student Avg Mark = CALCULATE ( AVERAGE ( ModuleResult[Mark] ) ). Better still, make it a measure, or compute it upstream if used for slicing.

items.symptom: The count of students with attendance below 70% is far higher than expected and includes students who have no timetabled sessions.
items.code:
Low Attenders =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER ( VALUES ( Student[StudentKey] ), [Attendance Rate] < 0.7 )
)
items.diagnosis: For students with no sessions, [Attendance Rate] is BLANK, and BLANK compares as zero, so BLANK < 0.7 is true.
items.fix: Add a blank test: FILTER ( VALUES ( Student[StudentKey] ), NOT ISBLANK ( [Attendance Rate] ) && [Attendance Rate] < 0.7 ).

items.symptom: The share of school headcount is 100 percent in every row.
items.code:
Share Of School =
VAR _Total = [Headcount]
RETURN DIVIDE ( [Headcount], CALCULATE ( _Total, ALL ( Programme ) ) )
items.diagnosis: _Total is evaluated once, in the current filter context, before CALCULATE runs. CALCULATE cannot change a value that has already been computed, so numerator and denominator are the same.
items.fix: Put the expression inside CALCULATE: DIVIDE ( [Headcount], CALCULATE ( [Headcount], ALL ( Programme ) ) ). Variables hold values, not expressions.

items.symptom: Offers show the same number as Applications in the grand total, even though many applications have no offer.
items.code:
Offers =
CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( Application ), USERELATIONSHIP ( Application[OfferDate], 'Date'[Date] ) )
items.diagnosis: With no filter on the Date table, nothing is excluded, so applications with a blank offer date are counted. Month rows exclude them only because the filter on Date drops the blank-date rows.
items.fix: Count the dates instead: CALCULATE ( COUNT ( Application[OfferDate] ), USERELATIONSHIP ( Application[OfferDate], 'Date'[Date] ) ). COUNT ignores blanks.

items.symptom: A slicer on Programme Level has no effect on the percentage of the school total.
items.code:
% Of School =
DIVIDE ( [Headcount], CALCULATE ( [Headcount], ALL ( Programme ) ) )
items.diagnosis: ALL(Programme) removes every filter on the Programme table, including the Level slicer, so the denominator is the whole school regardless of the selection.
items.fix: Remove only the filter you mean to ignore, for example REMOVEFILTERS ( Programme[Title] ), or use ALLSELECTED if the denominator should reflect the user's selections.

items.symptom: Enrolment dates in a UK departmental spreadsheet load with the day and month swapped for some rows (03/04/2025 becomes 4 March) and fail for others (13/04/2025).
items.code: Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes ( Source, { { "EnrolDate", type date } } )
items.diagnosis: The conversion uses the machine or service locale. If that is US English, text is read as month then day, so ambiguous dates are swapped and impossible ones error.
items.fix: Pass the culture explicitly: Table.TransformColumnTypes ( Source, { { "EnrolDate", type date } }, "en-GB" ), or Date.FromText ( [EnrolDate], [Culture = "en-GB"] ).

items.symptom: Refresh fails with DataFormat.Error: We couldn't convert to Number, in the Mark column.
items.code: Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes ( Source, { { "Mark", type number } } )
items.diagnosis: The source holds status codes in the Mark column, such as AB (absent) or EX (exempt), alongside numeric marks.
items.fix: Separate codes from marks: create MarkStatus from rows where the value is not numeric, and a numeric Mark using try Number.From ( [Mark] ) otherwise null. Keep the status so absences are not confused with zero.

items.symptom: After joining enrolments, module results and attendance in one query, headcount is right but total credits and attendance are far too high.
items.code:
select e.student_key, sum(r.credits) as credits, sum(a.attended) as attended
from enrolment e
join module_result r on r.student_key = e.student_key
join attendance a on a.student_key = e.student_key
group by e.student_key
items.diagnosis: Joining two fact tables to the same key multiplies rows: each result row pairs with every attendance row, so sums inflate by the other table's row count (a fan-out, or chasm, trap).
items.fix: Aggregate each fact to the student grain first (separate CTEs), then join the aggregated results to the student or enrolment table.
