items.name: Credit-weighted average mark
items.scenario: Weighted mean mark for a student, module or programme in the current context.
items.code:
Weighted Mean Mark =
VAR _Marked =
    FILTER ( ModuleResult, NOT ISBLANK ( ModuleResult[Mark] ) )
RETURN
    DIVIDE (
        SUMX ( _Marked, ModuleResult[Mark] * ModuleResult[Credits] ),
        SUMX ( _Marked, ModuleResult[Credits] )
    )
items.notes: Numerator and denominator use the same set of marked rows. Check local rules on resits (capped marks, best or latest attempt) and rounding.

items.name: First-attempt pass rate
items.scenario: Proportion of first attempts at or above the pass mark.
items.code:
First Attempt Pass Rate =
VAR _First =
    CALCULATETABLE ( ModuleResult, ModuleResult[AttemptNo] = 1, NOT ISBLANK ( ModuleResult[Mark] ) )
VAR _Passed =
    COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( _First, ModuleResult[Mark] >= 40 ) )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( _Passed, COUNTROWS ( _First ) )
items.notes: Pass mark is an assumption (40). Put it in a parameter table or a model property so it can differ by level (for example postgraduate).

items.name: Students who have passed a full year
items.scenario: Count students with at least 120 passed credits in the selected academic year.
items.code:
Credits Passed =
CALCULATE ( SUM ( ModuleResult[Credits] ), ModuleResult[Mark] >= 40 )

Students Passing Year =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER ( VALUES ( Student[StudentKey] ), [Credits Passed] >= 120 )
)
items.notes: A student who passes a module on resit has a failing and a passing row, and the failing one is excluded by the filter. Make sure a module cannot count twice if two passing attempts exist. Real progression rules (compensation, condoned credit) usually need upstream logic.

items.name: Attendance rate and low attenders
items.scenario: Attendance percentage and the count of students below a threshold, handling students with no sessions.
items.code:
Attendance Rate =
DIVIDE ( SUM ( Attendance[Attended] ), COUNTROWS ( Attendance ) )

Students Below 70% =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER (
        VALUES ( Student[StudentKey] ),
        NOT ISBLANK ( [Attendance Rate] ) && [Attendance Rate] < 0.7
    )
)
items.notes: Without the ISBLANK test, students with no timetabled sessions are counted as low attenders. Take the threshold from a parameter table.

items.name: New students in a term
items.scenario: Students in the current term who have no enrolment in any earlier term.
items.code:
New Students =
VAR _Now = VALUES ( Enrolment[StudentKey] )
VAR _Start = MIN ( Term[TermStartDate] )
VAR _Before =
    CALCULATETABLE (
        VALUES ( Enrolment[StudentKey] ),
        FILTER ( ALL ( Term ), Term[TermStartDate] < _Start )
    )
RETURN
    COUNTROWS ( EXCEPT ( _Now, _Before ) )
items.notes: Other filters stay active (programme, school), so a student new to the university but moving programme counts as new to that programme. Use INTERSECT for continuing students. For first-ever enrolment, compute a first-enrolment term flag upstream.

items.name: Academic year to date applications
items.scenario: Applications from the start of the academic year (or cycle) up to the latest date in context.
items.code:
AY To Date Applications =
VAR _ay   = MAX ( 'Date'[AcademicYearStart] )
VAR _last = MAX ( 'Date'[Date] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        [Applications],
        FILTER ( ALL ( 'Date' ), 'Date'[AcademicYearStart] = _ay && 'Date'[Date] <= _last )
    )
items.notes: When several academic years are in context, MAX picks the latest. For same-point-last-cycle comparisons shift _ay by one and align the day offset.

items.name: Mark band histogram
items.scenario: Count results in each band using a disconnected Bands table (Band, Lower, Upper) with bands such as 0 to 40, 40 to 50, 50 to 60, 60 to 70, 70 to 101.
items.code:
Results In Band =
VAR _lo = MIN ( Bands[Lower] )
VAR _hi = MAX ( Bands[Upper] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( ModuleResult ),
        NOT ISBLANK ( ModuleResult[Mark] ),
        ModuleResult[Mark] >= _lo,
        ModuleResult[Mark] < _hi
    )
items.notes: Lower is inclusive and Upper exclusive, so a decimal mark such as 69.5 falls in exactly one band. The blank test matters because BLANK compares as zero. Classification boundaries are institution-specific.

items.name: Offers by offer date
items.scenario: Count applications by the month the offer was made, not the month of application.
items.code:
Offers =
CALCULATE (
    COUNT ( Application[OfferDate] ),
    USERELATIONSHIP ( Application[OfferDate], 'Date'[Date] )
)
items.notes: Counting the date column excludes applications with no offer at every level, including the grand total. Repeat for AcceptDate.

items.name: Active enrolments as at a date
items.scenario: Students with an enrolment spanning the chosen as-at date, using a disconnected AsAt date table.
items.code:
Active Students As At =
VAR _asAt = MAX ( AsAt[Date] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        DISTINCTCOUNT ( Enrolment[StudentKey] ),
        FILTER (
            Enrolment,
            Enrolment[StartDate] <= _asAt
                && ( ISBLANK ( Enrolment[EndDate] ) || Enrolment[EndDate] >= _asAt )
        )
    )
items.notes: Open-ended enrolments have a blank end date. Define whether the end date is inclusive. Filtering the whole fact table can be slow at scale, so consider precomputing validity upstream.

items.name: Dynamic RLS by school
items.scenario: A Security table (Email, SchoolCode) maps staff to schools, and one role filters the School table.
items.code:
-- Filter expression on the School table in role "SchoolAccess"
CONTAINS (
    Security,
    Security[Email], USERPRINCIPALNAME (),
    Security[SchoolCode], School[SchoolCode]
)
items.notes: Staff with several schools simply have several rows. Plan for university-wide roles, test with View as and with real viewer accounts, and remember workspace roles with edit rights bypass RLS.

items.name: Date table with academic year
items.scenario: Calculated Date table for academic years starting 1 August.
items.code:
Date =
ADDCOLUMNS (
    CALENDAR ( DATE ( 2015, 8, 1 ), DATE ( 2035, 7, 31 ) ),
    "Month Number", MONTH ( [Date] ),
    "Month", FORMAT ( [Date], "MMM" ),
    "AcademicYearStart", IF ( MONTH ( [Date] ) >= 8, YEAR ( [Date] ), YEAR ( [Date] ) - 1 ),
    "Academic Year",
        VAR _s = IF ( MONTH ( [Date] ) >= 8, YEAR ( [Date] ), YEAR ( [Date] ) - 1 )
        RETURN _s & "/" & RIGHT ( FORMAT ( _s + 1, "0" ), 2 )
)
items.notes: Add an academic month number and sort Month by it. Mark the table as the date table. Academic year start is institution-specific, and many institutions already have a governed calendar upstream to use instead.

items.name: Unpivot assessment components
items.scenario: Turn Coursework, Exam, Practical columns into one row per component.
items.code:
Unpivoted = Table.UnpivotOtherColumns (
    Source,
    { "StudentID", "ModuleCode" },
    "Component",
    "Mark"
)
items.notes: Unpivoting other columns survives new component columns. Follow with a type step and handle status codes in Mark before converting to number.

items.name: Students with no enrolment
items.scenario: Find students in the extract that are missing from the Enrolment query.
items.code:
let
    Joined = Table.NestedJoin ( Students, { "StudentKey" }, Enrolment, { "StudentKey" }, "Match", JoinKind.LeftAnti ),
    Result = Table.RemoveColumns ( Joined, { "Match" } )
in
    Result
items.notes: LeftAnti returns left rows with no right match. For deterministic comparison, standardise the key in both queries first.

items.name: Parameterised academic year filter
items.scenario: Filter a source by an academic year parameter that can differ between Dev, Test and Prod.
items.code:
let
    Source = Sql.Database ( pServer, pDatabase ),
    Enrolment = Source{ [Schema = "mart", Item = "fct_enrolment"] }[Data],
    Filtered = Table.SelectRows ( Enrolment, each [AcademicYearStart] >= pFirstAcademicYear )
in
    Filtered
items.notes: A simple comparison against a parameter folds. Deployment pipeline rules can swap pServer, pDatabase and pFirstAcademicYear per stage.

items.name: UK date parsing
items.scenario: Convert text dates in dd/mm/yyyy format regardless of the machine locale.
items.code: Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes ( Source, { { "EnrolDate", type date } }, "en-GB" )
items.notes: Culture is the third argument. Without it, results depend on the locale of the machine or the service.

items.name: Final attempt per student per module
items.scenario: One row per student and module, using the latest attempt.
items.notes: Regulations decide whether the final mark is the latest attempt, the best, or a capped resit mark. Encode the rule once, in the warehouse.

items.name: Cohort retention in SQL
items.scenario: Entrants in 2023/24 who are enrolled in 2024/25.
items.code:
with entrants as (
    select distinct student_key
    from enrolment
    where academic_year = '2023/24'
      and entry_year_flag = 1
),
next_year as (
    select distinct student_key
    from enrolment
    where academic_year = '2024/25'
)
select
    count(*)                            as cohort,
    count(n.student_key)                as retained,
    count(n.student_key) / nullif(count(*), 0) as retention_rate
from entrants e
left join next_year n using (student_key)
items.notes: LEFT JOIN keeps cohort members who left, and COUNT over the right-hand key counts only matches. Exclusions and cohort filters (level, mode, domicile) must follow the agreed definition. entry_year_flag is a placeholder.

items.name: As-at join to a history dimension
items.scenario: Attach the department that applied when each result was recorded.
items.code:
select r.*, d.department_code
from module_result r
join dim_student_history d
  on  d.student_key = r.student_key
  and r.result_date >= d.valid_from
  and r.result_date <  coalesce(d.valid_to, '9999-12-31'::date)
items.notes: Half-open intervals prevent double matches at version boundaries. Add a dbt test that validity ranges do not overlap per student.

items.name: Cumulative applications by week
items.scenario: Weekly and cumulative application counts for the cycle.
items.code:
select
    date_trunc('week', application_date)                       as week_start,
    count(*)                                                    as applications,
    sum(count(*)) over (order by date_trunc('week', application_date)) as cumulative_applications
from application
where academic_year_start = 2025
group by date_trunc('week', application_date)
order by week_start
items.notes: A window function can wrap an aggregate. Add a partition by programme or school for per-group running totals.

items.name: Orphan and duplicate checks
items.scenario: Quick checks before loading a model.
items.code:
-- Fact rows whose school code is missing from the dimension
select count(*) as orphan_rows
from fct_enrolment f
left join dim_school s on s.school_code = f.school_code
where s.school_code is null;

-- Duplicate keys in a dimension
select student_key, count(*) as n
from dim_student
group by student_key
having count(*) > 1;
items.notes: In dbt these become relationships and unique tests. Track the counts over time rather than only failing the build.

items.name: Conditional aggregation pivot
items.scenario: One row per student and module with Coursework, Exam and Practical marks as columns.
items.code:
select
    student_key,
    module_key,
    max(case when component = 'Coursework' then mark end) as coursework,
    max(case when component = 'Exam'       then mark end) as exam,
    max(case when component = 'Practical'  then mark end) as practical
from assessment_component
group by student_key, module_key
items.notes: Each student and component pair should be unique, otherwise MAX hides duplicates. Snowflake also has PIVOT, but conditional aggregation is portable and easier to extend.

items.front: What is the difference between row context and filter context?
items.back:
Row context iterates a table one row at a time and lets an expression refer to the current row's column values. It exists in calculated columns and inside iterator functions (SUMX, FILTER, ADDCOLUMNS).
Filter context is the set of filters that decides which rows are visible to an aggregation. It comes from slicers, visual axes, page and report filters, and CALCULATE arguments.
items.trap: Row context does not filter anything. A row context on Customer does not restrict Sales unless context transition happens.

items.front: What is context transition?
items.back: When CALCULATE (or a measure reference, which is implicitly wrapped in CALCULATE) is evaluated inside a row context, the current row's column values are converted into filters in a new filter context. That is how an iterator can compute a per-row aggregate.
items.trap: Every measure reference inside an iterator triggers a transition, which is costly over high-cardinality tables. If the iterated rows are not unique, the transition filters on all columns, so duplicate rows are grouped together and counted together.

items.front:
What does a Boolean filter argument in CALCULATE actually do?
CALCULATE([Total Sales], Product[Colour] = "Red")
items.back: It is shorthand for a filter over ALL of that column: FILTER(ALL(Product[Colour]), Product[Colour] = "Red"). It replaces any existing filter on Product[Colour] rather than intersecting with it.
items.trap: A slicer on Colour = Blue is overridden, not combined. Wrap the filter in KEEPFILTERS to intersect. Boolean shorthand can only reference columns from a single table and cannot reference measures.

items.front: ALL vs REMOVEFILTERS vs ALLEXCEPT vs ALLSELECTED: what does each do?
items.back:
ALL: removes filters from a table or columns; also returns a table of distinct values when used as a table function.
REMOVEFILTERS: same filter-removal effect, but only valid as a CALCULATE modifier. It states intent more clearly.
ALLEXCEPT: removes all filters on a table except the listed columns.
ALLSELECTED: removes filters coming from the visual's own rows and columns but keeps the outer filters (slicers, page filters). Used for share of the visible total.
items.trap: ALLSELECTED depends on the visual and on shadow filter contexts, so results can surprise you. If you want the grand total regardless of slicers, use ALL.

items.front: SUM vs SUMX: when do you need the X version?
items.back:
SUM aggregates one column. SUMX iterates a table, evaluates an expression for each row, then sums the results. Use SUMX when the value needs a row-level calculation first, such as Quantity * Price.
SUM(Sales[Amount]) is effectively SUMX(Sales, Sales[Amount]).
items.trap: SUM(Sales[Qty] * Sales[Price]) is invalid because SUM takes a column reference. SUM(Qty) * SUM(Price) is valid but gives a different, wrong number.

items.front: Calculated column or measure: how do you choose?
items.back:
A calculated column is computed at refresh, stored in the model, and evaluated in row context. Use it for attributes you need to slice, filter, sort by or relate on.
A measure is computed at query time in filter context and stores nothing. Use it for anything that aggregates or must respond to user selections.
items.trap: Ratios and percentages built as columns then summed give nonsense totals. Calculated columns also add model size and refresh time.

items.front: What makes a good date table for time intelligence?
items.back: One row per day, contiguous with no gaps, covering whole calendar (or fiscal) years, unique non-blank date values of Date type, related to the fact table, and marked as the date table. It also carries the attributes you need: year, quarter, month, month number for sorting, fiscal fields.
items.trap: Relying on auto date/time creates a hidden table per date column and bloats the model. Using a fact table date column with gaps for SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and similar functions gives wrong or blank results.

items.front: How do you use an inactive relationship, and when would you?
items.back: Wrap the calculation in CALCULATE and add USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], 'Date'[Date]). The inactive relationship becomes active for the duration of that CALCULATE only. Typical case: role-playing dimensions such as order date versus ship date against one Date table.
items.trap: The relationship must already exist in the model as inactive. The alternative design is a separate date table per role, which suits cases where users must slice by both dates at once.

items.front: What does KEEPFILTERS do inside CALCULATE?
items.back: It stops a CALCULATE filter argument from replacing the existing filter on that column. The new filter is intersected (AND-ed) with the filters already in context instead.
items.trap: CALCULATE([Total Sales], KEEPFILTERS(Product[Colour] = "Red")) with a Blue slicer returns blank, because no row is both Red and Blue.

items.front: Storage engine vs formula engine: what is the difference and why does it matter for tuning?
items.back:
The storage engine (VertiPaq) scans compressed columns quickly and is multi-threaded for simple aggregations and filters. The formula engine handles the rest of DAX logic and is single-threaded. Fast queries push as much work as possible to the storage engine and keep materialised intermediate results small.
Tools: Performance Analyzer for visual timings, DAX Studio server timings for SE vs FE split, query plans for deeper analysis.
items.trap: Common causes of slowness: iterators over high-cardinality columns, nested iterators, measures referencing measures inside large iterators, high-cardinality columns in the model, and bidirectional relationships.

items.front: Why use variables (VAR) in a measure?
items.back: Readability, and each variable is evaluated once and reused, which can avoid repeated computation. A variable is evaluated in the filter context where it is defined, not where it is used.
items.trap: A variable defined outside CALCULATE keeps the outer context, so it will not respond to filters added inside the CALCULATE that uses it. This is the most common variable bug.

items.front: What is query folding and how do you check it?
items.back: Power Query translates steps into a single native query (for example SQL) that the source executes, so filtering, grouping and joining happen at the source rather than in the mashup engine. Check by right-clicking a step and seeing whether View Native Query is enabled, or with Query Diagnostics.
items.trap: Once a step breaks folding, every later step runs locally. Put foldable steps (filters, column selection) before non-foldable ones. Folding also matters for incremental refresh and for DirectQuery.

items.front: How do you set up incremental refresh, and what is the common filter mistake?
items.back: Create two DateTime parameters named RangeStart and RangeEnd, filter the date column with them, then define the refresh policy on the table (store N periods, refresh last M periods). The filter should fold so each partition queries only its own range.
items.trap: Use one inclusive and one exclusive boundary: date >= RangeStart and date < RangeEnd. Both inclusive duplicates boundary rows across partitions. The parameters must be exactly named and of DateTime type.

items.front: How is an M query structured, and what does lazy evaluation mean for it?
items.back: A let ... in expression: each step is a named value referring to earlier steps, and the in clause names the result. Evaluation is lazy and demand-driven: a step is only computed if the final result depends on it, and order of definition is not order of execution.
items.trap: Because evaluation is lazy, a source can be hit multiple times if a step is referenced more than once. Table.Buffer forces a table into memory to stabilise this, but it breaks folding for later steps and uses memory.

items.front: How do you handle errors in M?
items.back: try expr otherwise fallback for simple cases, or try expr to get a record with HasError, Value and Error fields for detail. For column-level issues, Table.ReplaceErrorValues, Table.RemoveRowsWithErrors, or Table.SelectColumns with MissingField.UseNull for schema drift.
items.trap: Errors in a column can sit unnoticed until refresh. Replacing errors with null silently hides data problems, so log or count them when it matters.

items.front: A left outer merge increased your row count. Why?
items.back: The right table has duplicate values in the join key, so each left row matches several right rows and the expanded result multiplies rows. Check key uniqueness on the right side, deduplicate with Table.Distinct on the key, or aggregate before merging.
items.trap: A merge is not a lookup. Treat it as a join and verify the cardinality you expect.

items.front: Why a star schema for Power BI?
items.back: Narrow fact tables of measurable events at a declared grain, surrounded by dimensions holding descriptive attributes, joined by single-direction one-to-many relationships. It compresses well in VertiPaq, filters predictably, keeps DAX simple, and avoids ambiguous filter paths.
items.trap: Always state the grain of the fact table first. Interviewers use that as a quick test of modelling discipline.

items.front: Where should transformation and business logic live: warehouse/dbt, Power Query, or DAX?
items.back: Push logic as far upstream as is practical. Warehouse or dbt: cleaning, joins, conformed definitions and anything reused across reports (testable, version controlled, reusable). Power Query: light shaping when there is no upstream layer, ideally folding. DAX: logic that must respond to user filter context, such as ratios, time intelligence and dynamic aggregations.
items.trap: Answering "DAX for everything" or "Power Query for everything" signals inexperience. Name the tradeoffs: reuse, testability, refresh cost, and where the definition of the metric is owned.

items.front: How does row-level security work in Power BI, and who does it not apply to?
items.back:
Roles contain DAX filter expressions on tables. Filters propagate along relationships in the filtering direction. Dynamic RLS maps USERPRINCIPALNAME() to a security table. Test with View as in Desktop and in the service.
It restricts users with the Viewer role. Workspace Admins, Members and Contributors can see all data.
items.trap: Filtering a dimension does not secure data via a bidirectional route unless "apply security filter in both directions" is enabled. Test RLS with a real viewer account, not as the author.

items.prompt: A calculated column is added to the Customer table. The Sales table is related to Customer (one-to-many). What does the column show for each customer?
items.code: Customer Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])

options.why: This is the classic assumption. Row context does not filter related tables, so no per-customer filtering occurs without context transition.

options.text: The grand total of all sales, identical on every row
options.why: Correct. There is no CALCULATE, so no context transition, and SUM is evaluated with no filters on Sales.

options.text: An error because SUM cannot be used in a calculated column
options.why: SUM is valid in calculated columns. It just returns an unfiltered result here.
Sales has data and is unfiltered, so the result is not blank.

items.prompt: A slicer on Product[Colour] is set to Blue. What does this measure return?
items.code: Red Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], Product[Colour] = "Red")

options.why: This would happen only with KEEPFILTERS, which intersects the filters.
The slicer filter on Colour is replaced by the measure's filter, not kept.
Correct. The Boolean argument is FILTER(ALL(Product[Colour]), ...) and overrides the slicer's filter on that column.

options.text: An error because the filter conflicts with the slicer
options.why: DAX does not raise conflicts between filters. It applies the override rules silently.

items.prompt: Which measure gives each product's share of the grand total across all products, while still respecting a slicer on the Region dimension table?

options.why: Always returns 1 where there are sales.
ALL(Sales) clears filters on the fact table's own columns only. Filters on the Product table still propagate to Sales, so the denominator is not the grand total.
Correct. It removes the product filters from the denominator and leaves the Region filter intact.
ALL() with no arguments clears every filter, including the Region slicer, which breaks the requirement.

items.prompt: Sales has Quantity and UnitPrice columns but no revenue column. Which measure returns total revenue?

options.why: Invalid. SUM accepts a column reference, not an expression.
Valid syntax, wrong maths. It multiplies the totals instead of summing row-level products.
Correct. SUMX evaluates the expression per row and sums the results.
Still invalid. CALCULATE does not change what SUM accepts.

items.prompt: What does DIVIDE([Numerator], [Denominator]) return when the denominator is zero and no third argument is supplied?

options.why: This is what the / operator does. DIVIDE exists to avoid that.
Correct. The optional alternate result defaults to BLANK.
Only if you pass 0 as the third argument.
The / operator can return Infinity for division by zero. DIVIDE does not.

items.prompt: Sales has OrderDate and ShipDate, both related to the Date table. OrderDate is the active relationship. How do you compute sales by ship date?

options.why: Correct, given the ShipDate relationship exists and is inactive. It activates for that CALCULATE only.

options.text: Swap which relationship is active whenever the report needs ship date
options.why: Not possible at report time, and it would break every other measure that relies on the active one.

options.text: Create a bidirectional relationship on ShipDate
options.why: Bidirectional filtering changes filter direction, not which relationship is used, and risks ambiguity.
This needs row context to resolve and does not respond to the Date table filter context properly.

items.prompt: A customer segment (Gold, Silver, Bronze) is derived from lifetime spend. It must be used as a slicer and be consistent across five reports built on different semantic models. Where should it be defined?

options.text: As a DAX measure in each semantic model
options.why: A measure cannot be placed on a slicer as a category, and five copies will drift.

options.text: As a calculated column in each model
options.why: Works, but five copies of the logic, no shared tests, and it adds refresh cost to each model.

options.text: Upstream in the warehouse or dbt layer as a column on the customer dimension
options.why: Correct. One governed definition, tested once, consumed by every model, and available as a normal attribute.

options.text: In Excel before the data is loaded
options.why: Manual, unversioned and not repeatable.

items.prompt: Source is SQL Server. Which step is most likely to break query folding?

options.text: Filtering rows on a column value
options.why: Translates to a WHERE clause.
Translates to a narrower SELECT list.
Translates to GROUP BY.

options.text: Adding a column that calls a custom M function with logic that has no SQL equivalent
options.why: Correct. The engine cannot translate arbitrary M, so folding stops at this step and later steps run locally.

items.prompt: Which filter is correct for an incremental refresh table?

options.why: Both ends inclusive, so a row exactly on a boundary lands in two partitions and is duplicated.
Correct. One inclusive and one exclusive boundary means every row belongs to exactly one partition.
Both exclusive, so rows exactly on RangeStart are dropped.
Matches only one instant, not a range.

items.prompt: RLS works when tested with View as, but a colleague who is a Member of the workspace sees all rows. Why?

options.why: RLS is not restricted to Premium.

options.text: RLS only restricts users with the Viewer role, not Admins, Members or Contributors
options.why: Correct. Workspace roles with edit rights bypass RLS, so share the app or report with colleagues as viewers to test properly.

options.text: The DAX filter expression is evaluated only once per day
options.why: Not how RLS works. Filters apply at query time per user.

options.text: RLS does not apply to imported data
options.why: RLS applies to import models. It is a core use case.

items.prompt: Given this Sales table, what does a table visual with Region on rows show for the three measures, including the Total row?
items.code:
Total = SUM(Sales[Amount])
All Regions = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALL(Sales[Region]))
Share = DIVIDE([Total], [All Regions])
items.explanation: East is 100 + 200 = 300 and West is 300. ALL(Sales[Region]) removes the region filter, so every row's denominator is 600. The Total row has no region filter, so Total and All Regions are both 600 and the share is 100%.

items.prompt: What rank does each product get?
items.code: Rank = RANKX(ALL(Product[Name]), [Total Sales])
items.explanation: RANKX defaults to descending order and to Skip for ties. B and C tie at rank 1, so the next rank is 3, not 2. Passing Dense as the ties argument would give A = 2 and D = 3.

items.symptom: A table visual shows Margin % per product correctly (about 30% each), but the Total row shows 2,400%.
items.code:
-- calculated column on Sales
Margin % = DIVIDE(Sales[Profit], Sales[Revenue])
items.diagnosis: The ratio is a row-level calculated column, and the visual sums the column. The sum of ratios is meaningless.
items.fix: Make it a measure: Margin % = DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Profit]), SUM(Sales[Revenue])). It recalculates in whatever filter context applies, including the total row.

items.symptom: Prior-year sales are blank or wrong for many periods. The measure uses the fact table's date column and the data has no sales on weekends.
items.code: PY Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Sales[OrderDate]))
items.diagnosis: Time intelligence functions need a contiguous date column. The fact table's OrderDate has gaps (and duplicates), so date shifting does not behave correctly.
items.fix: Build a proper Date table with every day, mark it as the date table, relate it to Sales[OrderDate], and use 'Date'[Date] inside SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR.

items.symptom: Refresh fails with: Expression.Error: The column 'Amount' of the table wasn't found. The source team renamed the column in a recent release.
items.code:
let
    Source = Sql.Database("server", "db"),
    Sales = Source{[Schema="dbo", Item="Sales"]}[Data],
    Picked = Table.SelectColumns(Sales, {"OrderID", "Amount"})
in
    Picked
items.diagnosis: Table.SelectColumns throws when a named column is missing. The step is not defensive against schema drift.
items.fix: Table.SelectColumns(Sales, {"OrderID", "Amount"}, MissingField.UseNull) returns nulls for missing columns so refresh succeeds, but add a check or data quality test so silent nulls are noticed. Better still, agree a contract with the source team or select from a stable view.

items.symptom: After merging Orders (10,000 rows) with Customers using a left outer join and expanding, the result has 10,450 rows.
items.code: Merged = Table.NestedJoin(Orders, {"CustomerID"}, Customers, {"CustomerID"}, "Customer", JoinKind.LeftOuter)
items.diagnosis: CustomerID is not unique in Customers, so some orders match multiple customer rows and expand into multiple output rows.
items.fix: Check the key with a Group By count, deduplicate Customers (Table.Distinct on CustomerID, or keep the correct current record), then merge again. Add a row count check after merges.

items.prompt: Explain context transition to a colleague who knows SQL but not DAX. Aim for 60 seconds.
keyPoints: Row context knows the current row but does not filter other tables
CALCULATE converts that row's values into filters
That is why a measure inside an iterator gives a per-row result
Measures are implicitly wrapped in CALCULATE
Cost and duplicate-row implications
A concrete example, such as per-customer sales in a calculated column

items.prompt: A stakeholder asks why their metric is calculated in the warehouse rather than in the Power BI report. Explain your reasoning.
keyPoints: One definition of the metric, reused by every report
Testable and version controlled (dbt tests, Git)
Reduces refresh and report load
Folding and DirectQuery implications

keyPoints.What does belong in DAX: context-sensitive logic such as ratios and time intelligence

items.name: Year-over-year growth %
items.scenario: Show percentage change in sales versus the same period last year.
items.code:
YoY % =
VAR _Current = [Total Sales]
VAR _Prior =
    CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( _Current - _Prior, _Prior )
items.notes: Needs a marked, contiguous Date table. DIVIDE handles a missing prior year. DATEADD('Date'[Date], -1, YEAR) is an equivalent alternative.

items.name: Running total
items.scenario: Cumulative sales up to the latest date in the current context.
items.code:
Running Total =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    FILTER (
        ALL ( 'Date'[Date] ),
        'Date'[Date] <= MAX ( 'Date'[Date] )
    )
)
items.notes: ALL on the Date column only removes filters on that column. Filters on other Date columns such as Year still apply, which usually gives a running total within the year. Use ALL('Date') to run across all years.

items.name: Percentage of total
items.scenario: Each product's share of the grand total, respecting other filters.
items.code:
% of Total =
DIVIDE (
    [Total Sales],
    CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], REMOVEFILTERS ( Product ) )
)
items.notes: REMOVEFILTERS(Product) clears product filters only. Use ALLSELECTED(Product) instead to get the share of the visible total.

items.name: Rolling 3-month sales
items.scenario: Sum of sales across the last three months ending at the current month.
items.code:
Sales Rolling 3M =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], MAX ( 'Date'[Date] ), -3, MONTH )
)
items.notes: Divide by 3 for an average only when all three months are complete and populated. Early months have fewer than three months of history.

items.name: Rank within category
items.scenario: Rank products by sales within each category.
items.code:
Rank In Category =
RANKX (
    ALLEXCEPT ( Product, Product[Category] ),
    [Total Sales]
)
items.notes: Iterates product rows that share the current category, so Product must be at one row per product. Add the Dense ties argument if gaps in ranking are not wanted.
